key_terms.meaning: The torque the operating field exerts on the moving element; it is proportional to I in a moving-coil meter and to I² in a moving-iron meter.
Opposing torque from a spring or from gravity; the pointer settles where deflecting torque equals controlling torque, fixing the scale.
Torque proportional to the speed of the moving element (air friction or eddy current) that stops the pointer quickly without swinging.
Moving-iron construction in which the coil magnetises an iron vane and pulls it into the coil, so the vane moves towards the stronger field.
Moving-iron construction with two iron vanes magnetised in the same direction; they repel each other and the movable vane turns.
An integrating instrument that multiplies power by time and counts kilowatt-hours; one kWh is one 'unit' on the bill.
An insulation resistance tester that applies a high DC voltage (commonly 500 V or 1000 V) and reads resistance in megaohms (MΩ).
Digital storage oscilloscope; it samples a signal, stores the samples in memory and displays the waveform, so one-shot and slow events can be seen.
A device that converts a physical quantity such as temperature, pressure or light into an electrical signal (voltage, current, resistance or frequency).
A transducer that generates its own emf from the measured quantity without an external supply, for example a thermocouple or a piezoelectric element.
A transducer that needs an external supply and works by changing its resistance, inductance or capacitance, for example a strain gauge or an RTD.
V_H = B·I / (n·q·t), where B is flux density in tesla, I is current in amperes, n is carrier density per m³, q is carrier charge in coulombs and t is plate thickness in metres.
A non-contact sensor that switches its output when an object comes within a set distance; inductive types sense metals, capacitive types sense most materials, optical types sense by light beam.
The difference in switching or output level when the same input is reached from the increasing side compared with the decreasing side.
The part of the bill equal to rupees per kWh multiplied by the units consumed in the billing period.
A monthly charge based on sanctioned load in kW (or kVA); it is paid whether or not any energy is used.
An extra charge when the power factor falls below the value set in the tariff, because low power factor means larger current and larger losses for the same useful power.
A billing arrangement in which solar units exported to the grid are credited against units imported, and only the net difference is billed.
Miniature circuit breaker; it trips on overload by a thermal (bimetal) element and on short circuit by a magnetic element, and can be reset by hand.
Deliberately connecting exposed metalwork to the soil through a low-resistance path so fault current flows, the protective device trips, and the metal stays near earth potential.

takeaways: A moving-coil meter gives a deflection proportional to current and suits DC, while a moving-iron meter gives a deflection proportional to current squared and therefore works on AC and DC both.
Every indicating instrument needs three torques: deflecting to move the pointer, controlling to bring it back, and damping to stop the swing.
Energy meter, megger, DMM and DSO answer different questions: how much energy, how good is the insulation, what are V, I and R, and what does the waveform look like.
A transducer turns a physical quantity into an electrical signal; Hall sensors use a magnetic field and proximity sensors detect objects without touching them.
Electric power comes from non-renewable sources such as coal thermal and nuclear, and from renewable sources such as solar and wind.
Power is generated at 11-25 kV, stepped up for transmission, stepped down at substations, and delivered at 230 V single-phase or 400 V three-phase.
The bill is fixed charge plus energy charge plus fuel surcharge, with a penalty if power factor is low; an energy audit and rooftop solar both reduce the units bought.
Residential wiring uses live, neutral and earth with an MCB for overload and short circuit and an RCCB for earth leakage, and earthing is what makes those devices work.
bank_note: Long answers here are judged on construction-and-working explanations with a neat diagram, correct voltage levels at each stage of the power system, and a clean numerical layout for tariff and solar sizing questions.

bank.q: Draw the construction of a moving-coil (permanent-magnet moving-coil) instrument and explain how the deflecting, controlling and damping torques are produced. Explain why it indicates only on DC.
outline: Parts: permanent magnet with curved poles, soft-iron core, coil on an aluminium former, spiral springs, pointer and scale
Deflecting torque from force F = B·I·l·N on coil sides, so torque is proportional to current — a linear scale
Controlling torque from the spiral springs, so deflection θ = k·I
Damping by eddy currents induced in the aluminium former, giving torque proportional to speed
On AC the torque reverses every half cycle and the inertia averages it to zero, so the pointer stays at zero; a rectifier is needed for AC

bank.q: Explain the construction and working of a repulsion-type moving-iron instrument with a sketch. Show that its deflecting torque is proportional to the square of the current, and state why it can be used on AC as well as DC.
outline: A fixed coil, a fixed iron vane inside it, and a movable iron vane on the spindle
Both vanes are magnetised in the same direction by the coil field, so like poles face each other and they repel
Force depends on the strength of both magnets, hence torque proportional to I², giving a non-uniform (squared) scale
Reversing the current reverses both magnetisms, so the direction of repulsion stays the same — this is why it works on AC and DC
Damping by air friction and control by springs or gravity; mention the advantages: robust, cheap, can carry overload

bank.q: Describe the construction and working of a megger. How is it used to test the insulation resistance of a domestic wiring installation, and what readings would you call acceptable?
outline: Hand-driven DC generator or electronic inverter producing a high test voltage, commonly 500 V for low-voltage wiring
Deflecting and controlling coils connected so that the pointer reads the ratio of current to voltage, i.e. resistance directly in MΩ
Test between live and earth, neutral and earth, and live and neutral with the supply switched off and loads disconnected
Very high reading means good insulation; a low reading (a few hundred kilohms or less) shows moisture or damaged insulation
Precautions: isolate the circuit, discharge after the test, never test a live circuit

bank.q: List the main conventional and renewable sources of electric power and explain the energy conversion in each. Give two advantages and two limitations of solar and of wind power.
outline: Conventional: coal thermal (chemical to heat to steam to mechanical to electrical), nuclear (fission heat to steam), large hydro (potential energy of water)
Renewable: solar photovoltaic (light to DC electricity), solar thermal, wind (kinetic to rotational to electrical via turbine and generator), small hydro, biomass
Solar: advantage — no fuel, low maintenance, works as distributed rooftop generation; limitation — only in daylight, large area per kW, output falls on cloudy days
Wind: advantage — no fuel, low running cost, good at windy sites; limitation — intermittent, noise and land use, needs a windy site
Note grid issues: variability of renewables needs backup or storage

bank.q: A house has a sanctioned load of 4 kW and consumes 320 units in a month. The tariff is: fixed charge ₹50 per kW per month, energy charge ₹6.50 per unit for the first 200 units and ₹7.50 per unit beyond that, fuel surcharge 8 paise per unit, and meter rent ₹40 per month. Calculate the fixed charge, energy charge, fuel surcharge, and total bill, and state the average cost per unit.
outline: Fixed charge = 4 × 50 = ₹200
Fuel surcharge = 320 × 0.08 = ₹25.60
Average cost per unit = 2465.60 / 320 ≈ ₹7.71 per unit; comment that the fixed charge makes the average rate fall as consumption rises

bank.q: A home uses 300 units (kWh) per month. Design a rooftop solar plant for it, stating the kWp capacity, approximate roof area, inverter rating, and how net metering reduces the bill. State the assumptions you make.
outline: Daily energy = 300 / 30 = 10 kWh per day
Assume about 4 to 4.5 kWh generated per kWp per day in Indian conditions, so capacity ≈ 10 / 4.2 ≈ 2.4 kWp, rounded to a standard 3 kWp
Area: about 8 to 10 m² of shadow-free roof per kWp, so roughly 25-30 m²
Inverter rated close to array capacity, about 3 kVA; cabling, DC and AC isolators, and an energy meter with export facility

Net metering: units exported in the afternoon are credited against units imported at night, so only the net import is billed; mention the applicable subsidy reducing capital cost and the payback estimate

bank.q: You are asked to check a 230 V domestic socket. Describe how you would use a digital multimeter and a digital storage oscilloscope, stating the range settings, the probe connections and one safety precaution for each.
outline: DMM on AC volts range above 230 V (say 600 V AC), black probe to neutral/earth, red to live; read about 230 V rms
Continuity and resistance ranges for checking the earth path and blown fuses, with supply off
DSO: use a step-down isolation transformer or a differential probe; vertical scale about 100 V/div with a 10× probe, time base about 5 ms/div to show two or three 50 Hz cycles
From the display read peak value and check that peak = √2 × rms ≈ 325 V for 230 V rms, and observe the waveshape for distortion
Safety: never connect a scope ground clip to the live line, do not exceed the probe voltage rating, work with one hand where possible

bank.q: A conveyor line must count metal boxes passing a point at about 200 boxes per minute without touching them. Choose a suitable sensor, explain its working principle, state its output type (NPN or PNP) and explain how hysteresis prevents double counting.
outline: Inductive proximity sensor is the correct choice because the boxes are metal and no contact is allowed

Working: an oscillator drives a coil that produces a high-frequency field; a metal target entering the field causes eddy currents, which reduce the oscillation amplitude, and a trigger circuit switches the output
NPN output sinks current to 0 V (sinking), PNP output sources current from the supply (sourcing); the PLC input card must match
Hysteresis: switch-on distance larger than switch-off distance, so a box at the boundary does not chatter and produce multiple counts
Check switching frequency: 200 per minute is about 3.3 per second, far below typical sensor ratings; mention sensing distance and mounting

bank.q: Compare moving-coil and moving-iron instruments on scale, sensitivity, AC/DC capability, effect of stray fields, cost and overload capacity. Which would you choose on a panel that must show both AC and DC values, and why?
outline: Scale: uniform for moving coil, cramped at the start for moving iron because torque depends on I²
Sensitivity: moving coil is more sensitive; moving iron draws more power from the circuit
AC/DC: moving coil is DC only (or rectified AC); moving iron reads both because the torque depends on I²
Moving coil needs a strong permanent magnet and is costlier; moving iron is cheaper, simpler and more robust, with better overload capacity
Moving coil is affected by stray fields unless shielded; moving iron has weaker fields and is less affected
Conclusion: moving iron for a general AC/DC panel, moving coil where accuracy and a linear scale matter

bank.q: A fuse, an MCB and an RCCB are all called protective devices, yet they protect different things. Compare their operating principle, typical breaking time, and the fault each does not protect against. Explain why an RCCB is needed even when MCBs are fitted.
outline: Fuse: a thin element melts on overcurrent, one-time use, cheap, slow, discriminating by element rating
MCB: bimetal for overload plus solenoid for short circuit, resettable, definite breaking time from the trip curve
RCCB: a current transformer or core-balance transformer compares live and neutral currents; a difference above 30 mA (or 100 mA) trips it within milliseconds
An MCB does not protect a person: a 30 mA shock through the body may be far below the MCB rating, and a live-to-earth leakage through a body or wet wall may never reach it
The RCCB does not protect against overload or short circuit, and does not protect against line-to-neutral contact; hence both are used together
Add earthing: without a proper earth path the RCCB still works, but the fault current path and touch voltage depend on earthing

bank.q: Draw the layout of a power system from the generating station to a domestic consumer. Give typical voltages at each stage and explain why transmission is done at high voltage and distribution at low voltage.
outline: Generation at 11 kV to 25 kV, stepped up by the generator transformer to 400 kV, 220 kV or 132 kV
Transmission lines to the grid substation; primary distribution at 33 kV or 11 kV; distribution transformer at the locality
11 kV / 400 V substation with transformer, HT switchgear, LT busbar, MCBs and metering; then 400 V three-phase four-wire to the street
Consumer gets 230 V single-phase (one phase and neutral) or 400 V three-phase (three phases), with earth
Justification: transmission power = √3·V·I·cos φ, so raising V lowers I, and line loss = I²R falls as the square; low voltage at the consumer end is needed for safety and insulation

bank.q: A small workshop pays a power factor penalty and a large energy bill. Explain what an energy audit is, list four measures you would suggest, and evaluate how you would judge which measure to do first.
outline: Energy audit: a systematic record of where energy is consumed, comparing consumption per product or per m² against a benchmark

Measures: replace filament and fluorescent lamps with LED, improve power factor with capacitors, fix compressed-air and water leaks, replace old motors with efficient ones, use timers and occupancy sensors
Power factor correction reduces current, hence line loss and the penalty; payback is short if the penalty is being paid
Judge by investment, annual saving and payback period = cost / annual saving, and by which measure gives the largest saving for the least disruption
Also consider rooftop solar under net metering: it reduces energy charge but not fixed charge
Mention measurement: use an energy meter or a power analyser to get the baseline before and after

bank.q: Explain the need for earthing, describe plate earthing and pipe earthing with sketches, and explain step by step how earthing makes a protective device operate during a fault.
outline: Need: to hold exposed metal at earth potential, to give fault current a low-resistance path, to stabilise the neutral, and to protect against lightning and static
Plate earthing: copper or galvanised iron plate in a pit with charcoal and salt, connected by a strip to the equipment, with a watering pipe
Pipe earthing: a galvanised iron pipe of about 38 mm diameter driven to a wet depth, with a funnel and wire mesh for watering
Fault path: body of appliance → earth wire → earth electrode → soil → supply neutral earth, so fault current flows and the MCB or fuse trips
Touch voltage stays low because the metal is held near earth potential; mention measuring earth resistance and the target value of a few ohms

bank.q: Draw a wiring layout for a two-bedroom house showing the service entry, energy meter, main switch, MCB distribution board, light and socket circuits, and the earth wire. Select typical MCB ratings and state where an RCCB is placed and why.
outline: Service cable from the pole to the meter board, energy meter, main double-pole switch, then the distribution board
Separate circuits: 6 A MCB for lighting, 16 A MCB for power sockets, 20 A or 32 A for air conditioner or geyser
Wire sizes: 1.0 or 1.5 mm² for lighting, 2.5 or 4 mm² for sockets, with the earth wire of the same or the next lower size
RCCB of 30 mA placed at the incomer of the distribution board so it covers all circuits, after the main switch
Earth continuity to every socket and metal enclosure; separate neutral and earth bars; colour code live brown, neutral blue, earth green-yellow
Mention the IE rules idea that all circuits must be protected and the installation must be tested before energising

glossary.def: A device that measures and indicates the value of an electrical quantity such as current, voltage or power.
An instrument connected in series with a circuit to measure current; it must have very low resistance.
An instrument connected in parallel across two points to measure potential difference; it must have very high resistance.
Permanent-magnet moving-coil instrument; the standard moving-coil meter used for DC measurement.
A low-value resistor connected in parallel with a meter to carry most of the current and extend its range.
The number by which the meter reading is multiplied to get the actual value when a shunt or series resistance is used.
A meter that displays DC and AC volts, current and resistance as digits, usually with a 3½ or 4½ digit display.
An instrument that plots amplitude against time so the shape, peak value, frequency and distortion of a waveform can be seen.
Slow rotation of the disc with no load connected, controlled by a small brake magnet or a shading coil.
The smallest change in input that produces a detectable deflection, often quoted in ohms per volt for a voltmeter.
The smallest change a digital instrument can display, fixed by the number of digits.
How close the indicated value is to the true value, usually quoted as a percentage of full-scale deflection.
Resistance temperature detector, a passive transducer (such as platinum) whose resistance rises predictably with temperature.
A passive transducer whose resistance changes when it is stretched or compressed with the surface it is bonded to.
An active transducer made of two dissimilar metals that produces a small emf proportional to the temperature difference between its junctions.
Linear variable differential transformer; a passive inductive transducer that gives an AC output proportional to core displacement.
A non-contact sensor that detects metal targets by the eddy-current change in its oscillator coil.
A non-contact sensor that detects any material by the change in capacitance when an object enters its field.
Two output wiring styles: NPN sensors sink current to 0 V, PNP sensors source current from the positive supply.
The maximum load in kW or kVA that the utility agrees to supply; it sets the fixed charge.
A per-unit charge that recovers changes in the cost of fuel used by the generating stations.
Residual current circuit breaker; it trips when the current in live and neutral differs by more than its sensitivity, typically 30 mA.
Earth leakage circuit breaker; an older name for a leakage-current-operated protective device, often voltage-operated in old installations.
The metal plate or pipe buried in soil that connects the earthing conductor to the general mass of earth.
The potential difference a person would feel between an exposed metal part and the earth under fault conditions.
An assembly of transformers, switchgear and busbars that changes voltage level and routes power.
